title: Statistics Maintenance
description: Understand how SQL Server uses statistics for cardinality estimation and learn to maintain them for optimal query performance.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Statistics Maintenance**. Understand how SQL Server uses statistics for cardinality estimation and learn to maintain them for optimal query performance. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Statistics Maintenance and be confident in applying it to your projects.

blocks.text: Statistics are data objects that describe the distribution of values in a column or set of columns. The Query Optimizer uses statistics to estimate how many rows will be returned by various operations in a query plan. Accurate statistics lead to accurate cardinality estimates, which lead to optimal plan choices. Stale or missing statistics lead to poor estimates and suboptimal plans.

blocks.title: Statistics Are Critical
blocks.text: Statistics are often the hidden cause of performance problems. A query that runs fast one day and slow the next is frequently due to statistics becoming stale as data changes, causing the optimizer to choose a different, slower plan.

Every statistic object contains a header, a histogram, and optionally density vectors. The header stores metadata about when the statistics were created and how many rows were sampled. The histogram shows the distribution of data values in the first column of the statistic. Density vectors store information about the uniqueness of values in multi-column statistics.

terms.definition: A statistical snapshot of up to 200 data value ranges (steps) for a column, showing the frequency of values within each range.
Information about the distribution of values across columns in a multi-column statistic. Higher density means more duplicate values.
The number of rows the optimizer predicts will be returned by an operation. Derived from statistics using histograms and density vectors.
A database-level setting that automatically triggers statistics updates when a threshold of data modifications is reached.
A statistics update that reads all rows in the table, producing the most accurate histogram at the cost of I/O.

blocks.text: How Statistics Are Created and Updated

SQL Server automatically creates statistics on index columns and columns referenced in WHERE clauses. The auto update statistics threshold triggers a resample when a significant percentage of rows change. For large tables, SQL Server may use a partial sample rather than a full scan to keep the update fast, though this produces slightly less accurate statistics.

blocks.title: Auto Update Can Be Slow
blocks.text: Auto update statistics runs during query execution and can cause sudden, unpredictable performance spikes. For large tables, consider scheduling regular UPDATE STATISTICS with a full scan during maintenance windows.

blocks.title: Managing Statistics

blocks.text: Filtered statistics target specific data subsets, providing more accurate cardinality estimates for queries with selective predicates. For example, a filtered statistic on IsActive = 1 helps the optimizer estimate queries that filter active customers more accurately than a table-wide statistic.

blocks.title: Creating Filtered Statistics
blocks.code:
-- Create a filtered statistic for active customers only
CREATE STATISTICS Stats_ActiveCustomers_City
ON dbo.Customers (City)
WHERE IsActive = 1;

-- Query benefits from the filtered statistic
SELECT * FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE IsActive = 1
  AND City = 'Seattle';

blocks.caption: How SQL Server uses statistics to estimate query row counts and choose execution plans.
blocks.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[Query Submitted] --> B[Query Optimizer]
    B --> C[Check Statistics Exists]
    C -->|Yes| D[Read Histogram & Density]
    C -->|No| E[Create Auto Statistics]
    E --> D
    D --> F[Estimate Row Counts]
    F --> G[Choose Join Order & Algorithms]
    G --> H[Generate Execution Plan]

blocks.text: A robust statistics maintenance strategy balances accuracy with I/O overhead. Full scans provide the highest accuracy but are expensive for large tables. Sample scans are faster but may miss skewed data distributions. The right approach depends on your workload patterns and data volatility.

blocks.title: Maintenance Best Practices
items: Enable AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS and AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNC for OLTP databases
Schedule weekly fullscan updates for large, frequently changing tables during off-peak hours
Use filtered statistics on heavily partitioned or logically segmented tables
Monitor for performance regressions after large data loads or bulk operations
Set AUTO_CREATE_STATISTICS ON so the optimizer can create statistics on missing columns
Avoid updating statistics too frequently on static lookup tables

blocks.title: Diagnose Stale Statistics
blocks.description: Identify tables with stale statistics by examining when they were last updated and comparing that to data modification patterns.
steps: Query sys.dm_db_stats_properties to find the last update date and modification counts for statistics on a large table
Calculate the percentage of rows modified since the last update
Determine if the auto update threshold has been exceeded
Run UPDATE STATISTICS with FULLSCAN on an outdated statistic
Capture the execution plan of a key query before and after the update to compare cardinality estimates
blocks.expectedOutcome: You will observe improved cardinality estimates and potentially a different, more efficient execution plan after refreshing statistics.

items.question: How often should I update statistics?
items.answer: For heavily modified tables, weekly updates are common. For static lookup tables, monthly or even less frequent updates suffice. Enable async auto update for OLTP systems to prevent query-time blocking.

items.question: What is the difference between FULLSCAN and SAMPLE?
items.answer: FULLSCAN reads every row in the table, producing a histogram with 200 steps covering the full data range. SAMPLE reads a percentage of rows, which is faster but may miss outliers and skewed distributions.

items.question: Should I disable auto update statistics?
items.answer: Generally no. Disabling auto update shifts the responsibility entirely to manual maintenance. If you have a robust scheduled maintenance plan, you can disable auto update for predictable behavior, but most systems benefit from keeping it enabled.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: Statistics describe data distribution and drive cardinality estimation in the Query Optimizer
Stale statistics are a leading cause of unexpected query plan regressions
Auto update statistics triggers based on modification thresholds — large tables may use partial samples
Filtered statistics improve estimates for selective queries on segmented data
Schedule regular maintenance for large, frequently changing tables; enable async auto update for OLTP
blocks.takeaway: Statistics are the foundation of query optimization. Keeping them accurate is one of the highest-impact maintenance tasks a DBA can perform.

data.text: Comprehensive Code Example

This example demonstrates a production-ready implementation of **Statistics Maintenance**. Study the code carefully, paying attention to error handling, type safety, and best practices. Try running it yourself and experiment with variations to deepen your understanding.

data.title: Production-Ready Implementation: Statistics Maintenance
data.content: Complete working example demonstrating best practices and common patterns.
data.code:
-- SQL Example with Best Practices
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spent,
    AVG(o.order_total) AS average_order
FROM 
    sales.customers c
LEFT JOIN 
    sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND o.order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, GETDATE())
WHERE 
    c.is_active = 1
    AND c.created_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY 
    c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING 
    COUNT(o.order_id) > 0
ORDER BY 
    total_spent DESC
OPTION 
    (RECOMPILE);

-- Performance Tips:
-- 1. Use appropriate indexes on join columns
-- 2. Avoid SELECT * - specify only needed columns
-- 3. Filter early with WHERE clause
-- 4. Use JOINs instead of subqueries when possible

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Statistics Maintenance**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Statistics Maintenance**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
